[POLL]- What is the best modern DC/Marvel television series?
I personally would say Daredevil is the best DC/Marvel ( as well as one of the best shows in 2015 thus far) tv series

I recently watched Agent Carter, Agents of SHIELD, and Daredevil on my quest to view the existing Marvel Cinematic Universe in more-or-less chronological order from the perspective of the storyline. I'd say that Daredevil probably has the best story, maybe best film technique (though it is ridiculously dark - i mean literally, unrealistically low lighting everywhere), but I like Agents of SHIELD best of those three. Agent Carter was very nicely put together as well, I really liked the atmosphere and some of the references to the comics and the rest of the cinematic universe, but there just isn't enough of it - only eight episodes. In Agents of SHIELD there's character development, it ties in directly to the marvel movies, there's aliens and gadgets and spies and mystery and conspiracy and emotions and action, and there are two full seasons of episodes. It has it's issues, lots of ways it could be better. Overall though I enjoy it moreso than Daredevil or Agent Carter.

I haven't yet watched The Flash, and I don't know what other Marvel/DC shows there are currently, so bear that in mind.

Edit: i think i like the characters in Agents of SHIELD. I like Fitz, and I like Coulson, and I like Skye, and despite her being kind of weird I like Raina. It also has a lot of variety in general compared to the other two shows - though overall it follows a long story arc it still has an episodic feel to it where episodes are more or less self-contained. I didn't get the sense that Daredevil's episodes would really work that way on their own. I could be totally wrong here though because i didn't watch them out of order.

Edit2: i guess to sum up my feelings about the three shows, Daredevil feels like a movie that has been broken up into segments. There's just not enough Agent Carter. Agents of SHIELD has two seasons with lots of characters and cool sci-fi stuff.

Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. has been very enjoyable so far, mostly thanks to good casting and writing. The cinematography in Daredevil is great. Agent Carter is good, but they focus a lot on her struggle to be taken seriously in a male dominated workplace and I'm worried that will prevent the story from becoming as compelling as it otherwise might be.

I recently watched a documentary on Howard Zinn on Netflix and was amazed by the level of commitment to the movements he endorsed during his life. Hundreds of thousands of Americans rallied for Equal Rights and the ending of the War in Vietnam among other issues plaguing society at that time.

Unfortunately, that level of Political Activism appears absent in our current society, even though there our countless causes to rally behind... whether that be the unconstitutional surveillance committed by the NSA/FBI/CIA, the exponential increase of violence committed by our police force, the TTP, the growing inequality in America, etc.

Is it media manipulation that paints Americans as apathetic to all of these injustices or are we really all that complacent? If the latter is true, how do we solve this problem?
What caused the drop in the level of Civil Disobedience experienced in America? The Anti-War/Civil Rights Movements of the 60s/70s appear as our apex of Activism; How can we get to that level again?

Howard Zinn is an exception, far from the rule. His politicism was criticized by his constituents in his field for taking such open stands and encourage his students to have open political opinions in history courses. Thinkprogress, rootsteikers, the EFF and Publicknowledge all have activists like this, but are at best the fringe of politics in the US.

Its hard to win against behemoth corporate funding with enough cash to sink an opinion in legal fees or by smear ads. Occupy was the single biggest movement in recent history and its criticized ad failing because of collapsed leadership-- and while this played a role the privatization of public spaces was eventually what evicted everyone from tent city. More engagement = more activism and we are entering an age of the echo chamber, just look over at reddit for what happens when communities hit critical mass and money can begin shaping discourse again.

One aspect of this is that the police now have a lot more ways to arrest you. The media tends not to cover it either - a civil disobedience protest is not as interesting (read: money-making) as the looting of a Walgreens. There is a definite narrative surrounding protests these days, that participants are just rowdy criminals who want to profit off of it. All of this has significantly decreased the power of a good old fashioned sit-in.

My personal theory based on not much more than gut feeling and unicorns: While the average American is taking home less pay on average, a great majority of us are enjoying a much higher standard of living than back when these movements were at the forefront. To put it bluntly, we're all getting fat and we're all fucking. If you're not getting fat, and you're not fucking, you're getting angry, Now of course there are small pockets of people like in Baltimore that are not getting fat and/or fucking and getting pretty angry but, for better or worse, this is a significantly small percentage of the population.

Also, the inequality is much less apparent. Whereas as a black person you wouldn't be able to sit in the front of the bus, use the same utilities (water fountains, amusement parks), weren't offered the same opportunities and had to deal with police brutality there now just are some distant very wealthy people. These extremely wealthy people aren't in your face every day treating you badly. Inequality is probably one of the strongest drivers of protest and it just isn't strong enough now.

I'd like to know how people managed to protest while also maintaining the essentials of life - shelter and food.

I strongly believe the main thing holding people back today is not complacency but an inability to act. We're all tied to our jobs and taking any relevant period of time off means you likely are not only going to be unable to pay rent (which could result in legal troubles and ruined credit given the lengthy contracts we're obligated to sign) but will have no direct means of feeding yourself and your family. Not to mention most people would likely be fired for taking any meaningful amount of time off for political action.

This isn't even just about the consequences on individuals trying to participate, but also the protests themselves. For instance when the Occupy movement started to gain in momentum the government cracked down on them primarily by simply denying them the ability to shelter themselves publicly anywhere. That took the legs out of the movement overnight. What was different in the past?

At least where I live, most blue collar workers don't get any special protection. If your employer doesn't want to give you time off, or doesn't approve of your activities during your time off, they can fire you legally. You might collect worker's compensation for a limited time, if you qualify, but that is the end of it.

Looking at other western countries there has been a rather unique massive protest very recently in France, caused by the attack on Charlie Hebdo. The difference between that and the issues you mentioned is that the attack on Hebdo happened in a very small period of time, was unexpected, against something that the people of France all felt strongly about (freedom of speech) and the damage could be witnessed was shocking and visible to all. The issues you mention are on the background, there isn't an unexpected massive incident to spark outrage and there is disagreement within the population on what the problem is. I think that for a massive protest you need these issues to build and build up until it reaches a level where an incident can blow it up.

To look back at history and specifically the Civil Rights Movement there was a lot of effort being put into orchastring for example the Rosa Parks protests. There were other black women that did the same as Rosa Parks before her, but weren't given attention by the NAACP because they for example were single moms. They chose to use the Rosa Parks story as their spark to ignite protests, something for people to rally around. This was the case with Michael Brown as well and more importantly, the full black community, or everyone that identified as black agreed with it and it was from that position of identity that people protested. In regards to your issues there is too much disagreement within the identity of 'American' or any other identity from which a protest could be sparked.

In short I think it is because you either need more fuel, a spark and/or a united and large enough identity for protests to begin.
